candidacyEngagementWeight.citation: Political interest is the strongest predictor of considering a run for office (Lawless and Fox 2010, It Still Takes a Candidate, Cambridge University Press, ch. 3). Weight on the person's engagement (0 to 1, from CES newsint). Spread 1 to 3. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyCauseWeight.citation: A personal stake in an issue moves people to run (Lawless and Fox 2010, ch. 4; Fox and Lawless 2005, American Journal of Political Science 49(3):642-659). Weight on the person's strongest recorded drive. Spread 1 to 3. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyTemperamentWeight.citation: Competitiveness, risk-taking and comfort with conflict raise ambition (Lawless and Fox 2010; Dynes, Hassell and Miles 2019, Political Behavior 41:309-336). Weight on the mean of sociability, risk and conflict, each -2 to 2, scaled to -1 to 1. Spread 0.5 to 2. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyMoneyWeight.citation: The cost of running deters candidates with less money (Carnes 2018, The Cash Ceiling, Princeton University Press). Weight on cash on hand against the filing fee, -1 to 1. Spread 0.5 to 2. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyTimeWeight.citation: Working-class people run less, partly for lack of time off work (Carnes 2018, ch. 3). Weight on the person's recorded daily work hours over a full shift. Spread 0.5 to 2. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyFullShiftHours.citation: A full-time shift of 8 hours a day (BLS: full-time is 35 or more hours a week).

candidacyAgeWeight.citation: Weight of the age term. Spread 0.5 to 2. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. candidacyAgeCenter.citation: Local elected officials are older than the adult population; the median age of city council members in the National League of Cities' surveys is in the mid-fifties.
candidacyAgeCenter.estimatedFrom: National League of Cities city council surveys; spread 50 to 60

candidacyAgeSpread.citation: How quickly the age term falls away from its center, in years. Spread 10 to 20. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no published coefficient on this scale: Lawless and Fox (2010), Fox and Lawless (2005) and Carnes (2018) give directions only, so the ordering (interest and a personal cause strongest) is kept.

candidacyStayOutPull.citation: The pull of staying out, against which running is weighed. Checked so that about half a percent of adults in a town choose to run for a local seat in a cycle: a few candidates for each of a town's handful of council seats (Ballotpedia's local election analyses report most local seats with one or two candidates). Spread 3 to 5. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): Kept at 4.2. Plausibility check, derived and not published: about 585,000 local elected positions (Ballotpedia 2022), 3-4 year terms and 1.5-2 candidates per seat give roughly 0.4-0.5% of adults as candidates in a four-year window, consistent with the 0.5% target.

candidacyIncumbencyWeight.citation: The pull of holding the seat already. Calibrated so about 81% of incumbents run again: from 2010 to 2024 an average of 18.8% of state legislative seats were open because the incumbent did not run (Ballotpedia, 'Early filing deadlines show fewer state legislative incumbents retiring than in previous years', May 1, 2024, https://news.ballotpedia.org/2024/05/01/early-filing-deadlines-show-fewer-state-legislative-incumbents-retiring-than-in-previous-years/). In a generated town (seed candidacy-a), 200 residents each holding a seat: 3 gives 73.5% running again, 3.5 gives 88%; 3.25 gives 83%. Spread 3 to 3.5. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): Kept at 3.25, which fits state legislators (81% run again). Large-district school boards run again only 62-68% (Ballotpedia, largest 200 districts, 2020-2023), so the value should vary by office.
